query: Starting from a eutectic high-entropy alloy with a hierarchical microstructure of dual-phase lamellar colonies, what single intervention could overcome limited room-temperature tensile ductility and brittleness while retaining or increasing strength? The hypothesis should address the tendency for dislocation pile-ups near internal boundaries to produce local stress concentrations, microcracking, and catastrophic damage during straining. Specify the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted strength and ductility relative to the untreated starting material, the applicable testing and operating conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled, single-step cryogenic rolling followed by a short, rapid annealing treatment will refine the dual-phase lamellar microstructure and strengthen the semi‐coherent phase boundaries so as to reduce dislocation pile‐ups. This should lower local stress concentrations and delay microcrack formation during room-temperature tensile loading, thereby overcoming brittleness while maintaining or even increasing the alloy's high strength.
generation.material_initial_state: An as‐cast eutectic high‐entropy alloy (e.g., AlCoCrFeNi2.1) with a hierarchical dual-phase (FCC/L12 and B2) lamellar colony structure, in which semi‐coherent phase boundaries permit dislocation pile‐up leading to local stress concentrations.
generation.intervention: Apply a single-step cryogenic rolling process (e.g., with an 8–10% thickness reduction) immediately followed by a short-duration annealing treatment at an optimized temperature (around 600–700 °C) to partially recrystallize the FCC phase while retaining the fine lamellar structure.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature tensile testing under quasi-static loading; the process is conducted post-casting during thermo-mechanical processing; operating conditions remain within typical ambient temperature and strain-rate regimes used in prior studies.
generation.structural_mediator: A refined, ultrafine lamellar microstructure with enhanced chemical disorder and improved integrity of phase boundaries that better distribute dislocations during deformation.
generation.mechanism: Cryogenic rolling introduces a high density of dislocations while suppressing excessive recovery due to the low temperature. The subsequent rapid annealing facilitates partial recrystallization of the softer FCC phase and recovery of the hard B2 phase, thereby increasing interfacial strength. This engineered microstructure interrupts and distributes dislocation motion, reducing local pile-ups at the internal boundaries and thereby limiting stress concentration and microcrack nucleation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the untreated, as‐cast alloy, the intervention is expected to yield similar or higher yield and ultimate tensile strengths (e.g., yield strength ~1.4 GPa) together with an enhanced elongation (ductility increased by, for example, >20% in elongation to failure), overcoming room-temperature brittleness.
generation.baseline: The untreated eutectic HEA, which exhibits dislocation pile‐ups at semi‐coherent lamellar boundaries leading to stress concentrations, microcracking, and limited room-temperature tensile ductility.
generation.boundary: The benefits of the treatment are anticipated primarily under room-temperature, quasi-static conditions; deviations in processing parameters (e.g., excessive annealing causing over‐recrystallization) or vastly different strain rates/temperatures may reduce the predicted improvements.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative gains in ductility and strength depend on precise processing parameters. Over-annealing may mitigate strengthening benefits, and the optimum balance requires further experimental tuning.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples from the same batch of eutectic HEA: one set undergoing the proposed cryogenic rolling plus annealing treatment and a control set retaining the as‐cast microstructure. Conduct room-temperature uniaxial tensile tests on both sets and perform detailed TEM analysis to compare dislocation distributions. Additionally, analyze fracture surfaces for evidence of microcrack nucleation at phase boundaries.
measurements: Yield strength and ultimate tensile strength
Dislocation density and pile-up characteristics via TEM
Fracture surface morphology (e.g., microcrack presence and distribution)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the treated samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in dislocation pile-ups at phase boundaries or if there is no improvement (or a deterioration) in room-temperature tensile ductility or strength compared to the untreated control, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Nano-lamellar (L12 + B2) AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high entropy alloy (EHEA) was processed by cryo-rolling and annealing. The EHEA developed a novel hierarchical microstructure featured by fine lamellar regions consisting of FCC lamellae filled with ultrafine FCC grains (average size ~200–250 nm) and B2 lamellae, and coarse non-lamellar regions consisting of ultrafine FCC (average size ~200–250 nm), few coarse recrystallized FCC grains and rather coarse unrecrystallized B2 phase (~2.5 µm). This complex and hierarchical microstructure originated from differences in strain-partitioning amongst the constituent phases, affecting the driving force for recrystallization. The hierarchical microstructure of the cryo-rolled and annealed material resulted in simultaneous enhancement in strength (Yield Strength/YS: 1437 ± 26 MPa, Ultimate Tensile Strength/UTS: 1562 ± 33 MPa) and ductility (elongation to failure/ef ~ 14 ± 1%) as compared to the as-cast as well as cold-rolled and annealed materials. The properties of many metallic alloys are essentially related to the structure, morphology and chemical distribution of boundaries. In terms of atomic structure, the phase boundaries contained in eutectic dual-phase HEAs were supposed to be insufficient in prohibiting dislocations due to their semi-coherent nature, which is similar to those widely reported in NiAl dual-phase intermetallic alloys,. However, in-situ deformation tests revealed that dense dislocation storage can be achieved within FCC phases and dislocation walls were formed along phase boundaries. The unexpected strong interfaces are thought to be highly related to the chemically disordered distribution of multiple solution atoms at phase boundaries as well as in the matrix of HEAs. Particularly, an ultra-thin segregation zone of randomly distributed Cr atoms, typically less than 2 nm in width (Fig. 3b and S4), was detected near the phase boundary without forming complex intermetallic compounds, which were intrinsically brittle and would lead to stress concentration. Realizing improved strength–ductility synergy in eutectic alloys acting as in situ composite materials remains a challenge in conventional eutectic systems, which is why eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs), a newly-emerging multi-principal-element eutectic category, may offer wider in situ composite possibilities. Here, we use an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA to engineer an ultrafine-grained duplex microstructure that deliberately inherits its composite lamellar nature by tailored thermo-mechanical processing to achieve property combinations which are not accessible to previously-reported reinforcement methodologies. The as-prepared samples exhibit hierarchically-structural heterogeneity due to phase decomposition, and the improved mechanical response during deformation is attributed to both a two-hierarchical constraint effect and a self-generated microcrack-arresting mechanism. This work provides a pathway for strengthening eutectic alloys and widens the design toolbox for high-performance materials based upon EHEAs.
